newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Kosovo shadow looms over Serbia's political crisis.
newsitem.headline: Kosovo shadow looms over Serbia's political crisis.

text.p: Slobodan Milosevic shot to power with a promise to protect Serbs in Kosovo 10 years ago and he may turn to that volatile province again to master his worst political crisis.

A populist pledge of security for Serbs fearing attack by police in the Albanian-majority region was the route to authoritarian power for Milosevic who quickly became president of Serbia. Kosovo Serbs have never been beaten since.
Milosevic spoke at Kosovo Polje, scene of a catastrophic defeat of Serb forces by the Turkish army in 1389, and the symbolic home of Serbian nationalism.

Diplomats and independent domestic analysts fear Milosevic could now use the Albanian issue to castigate a rising Serbian opposition movement as a danger to national security and to prepare the ground for police repression.
Their worries stem from the renewed energy of the Albanian independence movement and a worrying rise in violence.
After Milosevic became president he abolished the autonomy of the impoverished Kovoso province, where ethnic Albanians outnumber Serbs nine to one.

Albanians dissented quietly, boycotting Serb institutions for eight years. But that relatively mild approach could change soon with Kosovo Albanian leaders like Adem Demaqi pressing for more radical action.
Violence against Serbs in Kosovo, especially security police, has resurged and the Serb rector of Pristina University in Kosovo was critically injured in a mysterious car bombing two weeks ago.
The Serbian state media accused the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition of complicity, which it denied.

Zajedno has led huge peaceful demonstrations over the alleged theft of its victories in municipal elections in 14 of Serbia's 18 largest cities, including Belgrade, in the biggest threat ever to Milosevic's Socialist dominance of Serbia.
Western diplomats say ethnic Albanians may try and mount the same type of peaceful protests Zajedno has been holding.
"Exactly what the doctor ordered. Milosevic would accuse Zajedno of fomenting unrest in Kosovo, jeopardising national security and use the pretext to crack down on both," a Western diplomat said.

"Goodbye to the pro-democracy movement in Serbia, but also to talk of peaceful negotiations for settling the Kosovo issue. Naturally, it would all be under the pretext of protecting the rights of the remaining Serbs in Kosovo."
Milosevic has had few qualms about turning his dreaded security police, and even tanks in 1991, on Serbs who dared to challenge Socialist power elsewhere in Serbia.
Today, police are beating opposition Serbs, sporadically enough to avoid a major international outcry for the time being.
The Socialists appear unshaken by the extent and size of Zajedno's protests which have drawn up to half a million people at their peak.

Zajedno protesters refuse to quit and the West has warned Milosevic to forget about economic aid without democratic reform. Backed into this corner, Milosevic may seek salvation in Kosovo, the region that once "created" him, analysts say.
Ruling Socialists are not budging on the issue as their hardliners press for police action to get protesters off the streets and look to Kosovo for the political signal.
